summary: Describes how to produce RSA/SHA-1 signature records and RSA key records in the Domain Name System. It completely replaces RFC 2537 for RSA keys. These records let DNS data be signed and verified in DNSSEC.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 3110 specifies how DNS resource records carry RSA public keys and RSA/SHA-1 signatures for DNSSEC. It replaced the earlier RSA/MD5 approach, defines the key and signature formats, and assigns them the same DNSSEC algorithm number.

questions: how to publish rsa keys in dnssec
what is rsa sha1 in dns
why was rsa md5 replaced in dnssec
subtitle: Specifies RSA public keys and RSA/SHA-1 signatures for DNSSEC records.

tldr.problem: DNSSEC needs a way to publish RSA public keys and signatures, and the earlier DNS RSA signature specification used the weaker MD5 hash.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines the RSA KEY record encoding and RSA/SHA-1 SIG record calculation, assigning algorithm number 5 to both.
tldr.outcome: It replaced RFC 2537 and made RSA/SHA-1 support mandatory for DNSSEC at publication time. RFC 3110 is later updated by RFC 6944.

today: RFC 3110 is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes RFC 2537 and is updated by RFC 6944.

sections.title: RSA Keys and Signatures in DNS
sections.content:
DNSSEC adds cryptographic keys and digital signatures to DNS data. RFC 2537 had described RSA keys and RSA/MD5 signatures, but the RFC reports concerns about the strength of MD5 and defines RSA/SHA-1 signatures instead.

RFC 3110 describes both the new signature record and the RSA public-key record needed to verify it. The document states that RSA/SHA-1 implementation is mandatory for DNSSEC and that generating RSA/MD5 signatures is not recommended.
sections.plainLanguage: DNSSEC uses published public keys to check signatures on DNS information. This RFC specifies an RSA signature using SHA-1 and the matching way to publish its public key.

sections.title: The RSA Public-Key Record
sections.content:
An RSA public key is stored in the DNS as a KEY resource record using algorithm number 5. Its algorithm-specific data contains an exponent length, the public exponent, and the modulus.

The exponent and modulus are each limited to 4096 bits for interoperability. A short exponent length uses one octet; longer lengths use a zero octet followed by a two-octet length. Leading zero octets are prohibited in both integers.
sections.plainLanguage: The DNS key record stores the RSA exponent and modulus with a length field for the exponent. The record's algorithm number identifies it as an RSA key for the signature algorithm in this RFC.

sections.title: How RSA/SHA-1 Signatures Are Stored
sections.content:
An RSA/SHA-1 signature is carried in a SIG resource record using algorithm number 5. The signer hashes the data with SHA-1 and applies the RSA private exponent to a formatted value containing the hash and a fixed algorithm prefix.

The public modulus must be at least 512 bits and no more than 4096 bits. The record uses the public key with the same algorithm number; the RFC changes the RSA KEY algorithm number used in RFC 2537 to match.
sections.plainLanguage: The signer calculates a SHA-1 hash of the DNS data and signs that hash with RSA. A resolver can use the published public key to check the signature.

sections.title: Key Size and DNS Response Size
sections.content:
The RFC discusses a small RSA public exponent as a way to reduce signature-verification work. It notes that exponent 3 is acceptable for a key used only for authentication, while 65537 is a more conservative choice for keys that might later serve other purposes.

Because DNS has traditionally favored small transfers, the document recommends reasonable efforts to keep key-record sets small while retaining adequate security. A secure zone also returns at least one authenticating signature record.
sections.plainLanguage: Key choices affect the work needed to verify signatures and the size of DNS responses. The RFC recommends balancing adequate security with keeping DNS key data reasonably small.

sections.title: Trusting Keys Retrieved from DNS
sections.content:
A key retrieved from DNS should not be trusted unless it came securely from a secure resolver or was independently verified, and the process meets the user's security policy. The RFC also says key strength depends on the application and local policy.

The SHA-1 signature format is an authentication mechanism, not a guarantee that every published key is trustworthy. Critical applications should consider available algorithms and key sizes according to their needs.
sections.plainLanguage: A DNS key is useful only if the user can trust how it was obtained. Secure resolution or independent verification is needed before relying on the key.
